stops.stop: Bunnefjord: the Fram leaves Norway with a false destination
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Roald Amundsen': the Fram left Norway on 3 June 1910). stops.stop: Buenos Aires: the patron on the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: Fram's arrival at Buenos Aires on 25 May 1912 is attested (Fram Museum, 'the-polar-ship-fram'). Whether Amundsen himself was aboard or ashore in Buenos Aires was not established in this pass; the stop is placed on the ship's movement and on his patron's presence there. Don Pedro Christophersen's patronage is a reconstruction, and the mountain named for him is not verified in this pass. The pin is the canonical Buenos Aires anchor used across the atlas, not the geography lens's -58.3705. CORRECTED: Fram never reached San Francisco; she waited at Colon, was refused the canal transit, returned to Buenos Aires, and went home to Horten on 16 July 1914.

stops.stop: Ny-Alesund, Svalbard: N 24 and N 25 lift off the water
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum, 'the-n24-n25-flight-towards-the-north-pole-1925'). Six men in two Dornier Wal flying boats, with Lincoln Ellsworth financing and Hjalmar Riiser-Larsen and Leif Dietrichson among the pilots.

stops.segment: The Flying Boats and the Airship
stops.stop: Eighty-seven degrees forty-three minutes north: a runway cut in moving ice
stops.date_confidence: DATES CORRECTED. The pool attributed a 22 May landing and a 6 June takeoff to Britannica; the Fram Museum's N24/N25 page gives the forced landing on 21 May 1925, the same day they left, after more than eight hours of flight, and the takeoff on 15 June 1925, about three and a half weeks later. A 6 June takeoff also contradicts the pool's own 'over three weeks'. The longitude of the landing is not independently confirmed.

stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Fram Museum, 'the-norge-flight-1926'). CORRECTED: the pool called Nobile the airship's commander. Nobile designed the airship and served as its pilot; Amundsen led the expedition (Wikipedia, 'Norge (airship)'). Financing was Ellsworth together with the Norsk Luftseiladsforening, not Ellsworth alone. The 11 May 1926 departure from Ny-Alesund at 09:55 is carried in this campa. The pin is the geographic pole, the same 90.0 / 0.0 used elsewhere in the atlas.

stops.stop: Tromso: the Latham 47 takes off and is not heard again
stops.date_confidence: attested (Britannica; Wikipedia, 'Latham 47'). Radio contact was lost within hours of departure. The assessment of the aircraft as an untested prototype for the conditions comes from Karen May and George Lewis in Polar Record.

stops.segment: The Latham and the Empty Sea
stops.stop: The coast off Troms: a float comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Latham 47': the torn-off port float found off the coast of Troms, 31 August 1928). CONTRADICTION NOT RESOLVED: the pool's Fram Museum-derived chronology reads the recovered artifacts as indicating a crash south of Bjornoya, while the Latham 47 article draws no conclusion at all and says the aircraft disappeared without a trace. Both float and fuel tank came ashore south of Bjornoya, off mainland Norway, which is consistent with drift and establishes no crash site. The file records no crash location. The pin is an approximate position on the Troms coast.
